{{DISPLAYTITLE:Quotient types}}
{{Plebeian|Lean theorem prover/Explainers/What the axioms are}}
{{Lean theorem prover map}}

A '''quotient type''' is a type whose elements are those of an existing type, with every
pair related by a given relation made equal. Mathematics constructs such objects constantly:
the integers modulo <math>n</math>, rational numbers as fractions up to cancellation, finite
sets as lists up to order and repetition. Lean provides quotients as a primitive of its type theory: four
constants, one axiom and one computation rule. This page sets out those rules, the
<code>Setoid</code> and <code>Quotient</code> layer built on them, a worked example, and
what the computation rule buys.

== The primitives ==

The constants are introduced early in Lean's core library by a dedicated command,
<code>init_quot</code>, not by an inductive definition.<ref name="prelude">Lean 4 source, file <code>src/Init/Prelude.lean</code>, version 4.34.1: the <code>init_quot</code> command and the documentation of <code>Quot</code>, <code>Quot.mk</code>, <code>Quot.lift</code>, <code>Quot.ind</code>, <code>Quot.sound</code> and <code>Quot.lcInv</code>. Apache License 2.0. https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/blob/v4.34.1/src/Init/Prelude.lean</ref> Lean prints
them so:

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#print Quot
#check @Quot.mk
#check @Quot.lift
#check @Quot.ind
#check @Quot.sound
</pre>
<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
Quotient primitive Quot.{u} : {α : Sort u} → (α → α → Prop) → Sort u
@Quot.mk : {α : Sort u_1} → (r : α → α → Prop) → α → Quot r
@Quot.lift : {α : Sort u_1} →
  {r : α → α → Prop} → {β : Sort u_2} → (f : α → β) → (∀ (a b : α), r a b → f a = f b) → Quot r → β
@Quot.ind : ∀ {α : Sort u_1} {r : α → α → Prop} {β : Quot r → Prop}, (∀ (a : α), β (Quot.mk r a)) → ∀ (q : Quot r), β q
@Quot.sound : ∀ {α : Sort u_1} {r : α → α → Prop} {a b : α}, r a b → Quot.mk r a = Quot.mk r b
</pre>

As rules: for any relation <math>r</math> on <math>A</math> there is a type, and every
element of <math>A</math> gives an element of it,

:<math>\frac{\Gamma \vdash A : \mathrm{Sort}\,u \quad \Gamma \vdash r : A \to A \to \mathrm{Prop}}{\Gamma \vdash \mathrm{Quot}\,r : \mathrm{Sort}\,u} \qquad \frac{\Gamma \vdash a : A}{\Gamma \vdash \mathrm{Quot.mk}\,r\,a : \mathrm{Quot}\,r}</math>

A function out of the quotient is a function out of <math>A</math> together with a proof
that it respects <math>r</math>:

:<math>\frac{\Gamma \vdash f : A \to B \quad \Gamma \vdash h : \Pi (a\,b : A).\, r\,a\,b \to f\,a = f\,b}{\Gamma \vdash \mathrm{Quot.lift}\,f\,h : \mathrm{Quot}\,r \to B}</math>

and it computes on representatives:

:<math>\mathrm{Quot.lift}\,f\,h\,(\mathrm{Quot.mk}\,r\,a) \equiv f\,a</math>

The induction principle <code>Quot.ind</code> says that, for proving a proposition, every
element may be taken to be some <code>Quot.mk r a</code>. Finally the axiom identifies
related representatives:

:<math>\frac{\Gamma \vdash p : r\,a\,b}{\Gamma \vdash \mathrm{Quot.sound}\,p : \mathrm{Quot.mk}\,r\,a = \mathrm{Quot.mk}\,r\,b}</math>

'''Only <code>Quot.sound</code> is an axiom in any real sense.''' Carneiro observes that
<code>Quot</code>, <code>Quot.mk</code>, <code>Quot.lift</code> and the computation rule are all
satisfied by reading the quotient as <math>A</math> itself, <code>Quot.mk</code> as the
identity and <code>Quot.lift f h</code> as <code>f</code>; ''Theorem Proving in Lean 4'' notes
that <code>Quot.ind</code> holds under the same reading.<ref name="tpil" /> What that reading cannot satisfy is the identification of distinct
representatives. Because the computation rule is a reduction and not a constant, Carneiro calls
quotients a semi-built-in feature: Lean's kernel has to know about them, and they are
switched on as a whole.<ref name="carneiro">Mario Carneiro, ''The Type Theory of Lean'', Master's thesis, Carnegie Mellon University, 2019; §2.7.1 (p. 13), §2.8 (p. 15) and §3.1.1 (p. 17). https://github.com/digama0/lean-type-theory/releases/tag/v1.0</ref>

The relation need not be an equivalence relation. The rules for <code>Quot</code> and
<code>Eq</code> together make equality in <code>Quot r</code> the equivalence relation
generated by <math>r</math>.<ref name="refman-quot">''The Lean Language Reference'', version 4.34.0, §4.5 "Quotients": the introduction, §4.5.5 "Logical Model", §4.5.5.2 "Quotients and Inductive Types", §4.5.6 "Quotients and Function Extensionality" and §4.5.7 "Squash Types". https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/4.34.0/The-Type-System/Quotients/</ref>

== An example: unordered pairs ==

An unordered pair is an ordered pair taken up to swapping its components. The relation
below holds when one pair is the other reversed. It is symmetric but not reflexive, and
<code>Quot</code> does not mind.

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
/-- `p` and `q` are related when `q` is `p` with its components swapped. -/
def Swapped (α : Type) (p q : α × α) : Prop := p.1 = q.2 ∧ p.2 = q.1

def UPair (α : Type) : Type := Quot (Swapped α)

def UPair.mk {α : Type} (a b : α) : UPair α := Quot.mk (Swapped α) (a, b)

theorem UPair.mk_comm {α : Type} (a b : α) : UPair.mk a b = UPair.mk b a :=
  Quot.sound ⟨rfl, rfl⟩

def UPair.sum (u : UPair Nat) : Nat :=
  Quot.lift (fun p => p.1 + p.2)
    (fun p q (h : Swapped Nat p q) => by rw [h.1, h.2, Nat.add_comm])
    u

example : UPair.sum (UPair.mk 3 4) = 7 := rfl
#eval UPair.sum (UPair.mk 3 4)

theorem UPair.sum_pos (u : UPair Nat) (h : ∀ a b, UPair.mk a b = u → 0 &lt; a) :
    0 &lt; UPair.sum u := by
  induction u using Quot.ind with
  | mk p => exact Nat.lt_of_lt_of_le (h p.1 p.2 rfl) (Nat.le_add_right _ _)

#print axioms UPair.mk_comm
#print axioms UPair.sum
#print axioms UPair.sum_pos
</pre>
<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
7
'UPair.mk_comm' depends on axioms: [Quot.sound]
'UPair.sum' does not depend on any axioms
'UPair.sum_pos' does not depend on any axioms
</pre>

Each primitive has its part. <code>UPair.mk_comm</code> is the one statement that needs the
axiom: it asserts that two different representatives give the same element. The sum is
defined by <code>Quot.lift</code>, and the obligation it carries is the proof that swapping
the components does not change <code>p.1 + p.2</code>. A function that does not respect the
relation, such as the first component, cannot be lifted, because no such proof exists.
The <code>example</code> is closed by <code>rfl</code>: the computation rule reduces
<code>UPair.sum (UPair.mk 3 4)</code> to <code>3 + 4</code>, and then to <code>7</code>.
The theorem <code>UPair.sum_pos</code> uses <code>Quot.ind</code> to reduce a statement about
every unordered pair to one about representatives. Neither the definition nor the induction
uses an axiom; only the identification of representatives does.

== Setoid and Quotient ==

When the relation is an equivalence relation, the core library bundles it as a
'''setoid''': a type with a chosen relation and a proof that it is reflexive, symmetric and
transitive. <code>Quotient s</code> is then <code>Quot</code> applied to the setoid's
relation.<ref name="core">Lean 4 source, file <code>src/Init/Core.lean</code>, version 4.34.1: the definitions of <code>Setoid</code>, <code>Quotient</code> and <code>Quotient.exact</code>. Apache License 2.0. https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/blob/v4.34.1/src/Init/Core.lean</ref>

<pre class="lean" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
#print Setoid
#print Quotient

instance parity : Setoid Nat where
  r a b := a % 2 = b % 2
  iseqv := ⟨fun _ => rfl, fun h => h.symm, fun h₁ h₂ => h₁.trans h₂⟩

def Mod2 : Type := Quotient parity

def Mod2.ofNat (n : Nat) : Mod2 := Quotient.mk parity n

def Mod2.isOdd : Mod2 → Bool :=
  Quotient.lift (fun n => n % 2 == 1) (fun a b (h : a % 2 = b % 2) => by rw [h])

example : Mod2.ofNat 3 = Mod2.ofNat 7 := Quotient.sound rfl
example : Mod2.isOdd (Mod2.ofNat 7) = true := rfl

theorem Mod2.two_ne_three : Mod2.ofNat 2 ≠ Mod2.ofNat 3 := fun h =>
  absurd (show 2 % 2 = 3 % 2 from Quotient.exact h) (by decide)

#print axioms Mod2.two_ne_three
</pre>
<pre class="lean-output" style="background: #ffffff; border: 1px dashed #a2a9b1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
class Setoid.{u} (α : Sort u) : Sort (max 1 u)
number of parameters: 1
fields:
  Setoid.r : α → α → Prop
  Setoid.iseqv : Equivalence Setoid.r
constructor:
  Setoid.mk.{u} {α : Sort u} (r : α → α → Prop) (iseqv : Equivalence r) : Setoid α
def Quotient.{u} : {α : Sort u} → Setoid α → Sort u :=
fun {α} s => Quot Setoid.r
'Mod2.two_ne_three' depends on axioms: [propext]
</pre>

<code>Mod2</code> is the integers modulo 2, built from the natural numbers. Showing that
<code>3</code> and <code>7</code> have the same class is <code>Quotient.sound</code> applied to
a proof that <code>3 % 2 = 7 % 2</code>, which holds by computation. Showing that
<code>2</code> and <code>3</code> have different classes needs the converse, that equal
classes come from related representatives. That is <code>Quotient.exact</code>, and it is
where the equivalence relation matters. Its proof lifts the relation itself to a
proposition-valued function on pairs of classes; the obligation is that related inputs give
equal propositions, which needs propositional extensionality, and reflexivity then closes
the argument.<ref name="core" /> The output records it: the proof that two classes differ
depends on <code>propext</code>, not on <code>Quot.sound</code>.

== What the computation rule buys ==

Because <code>Quot.lift</code> reduces on <code>Quot.mk</code>, a function defined on a
quotient computes. <code>rfl</code> proves <code>UPair.sum (UPair.mk 3 4) = 7</code>, and
<code>#eval</code> runs the same function. The reference manual contrasts this with working
directly on sets of equivalence classes: functions out of such sets need non-computational
classical principles, whereas functions out of a quotient are ordinary functions that also
respect a relation.<ref name="refman-quot" /> It also notes that the quotient leaves
definitional equality untouched: two elements of a quotient are definitionally equal exactly
when their representatives are.<ref name="refman-quot" /> Elements made equal by
<code>Quot.sound</code> are equal propositionally, by a proof.

The rule is also what makes [[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Propositional equality|function extensionality]]
a theorem. Quotienting a function type by pointwise equality and applying each class to an
argument reduces, by this rule, back to the original function. A propositional version of
the rule would not do, because using it under a binder would already need function
extensionality.<ref name="refman-quot" /> ''Theorem Proving in Lean 4'' likewise presents
function extensionality as a consequence of the quotient construction.<ref name="tpil">Jeremy Avigad, Leonardo de Moura, Soonho Kong and Sebastian Ullrich, ''Theorem Proving in Lean 4'', chapter 12 "Axioms and Computation", §12.3 and §12.4. https://lean-lang.org/theorem_proving_in_lean4/Axioms-and-Computation/</ref>

The compiler erases <code>Quot.lift</code>. The core library carries an unsafe constant,
<code>Quot.lcInv</code>, documented as the device for doing so,<ref name="prelude" /> and the
reference manual notes that <code>Squash α</code>, the quotient of <code>α</code> by the
relation that relates everything, is represented at run time exactly as <code>α</code>
is.<ref name="refman-quot" />

== Limits ==

<code>Quot</code> is not an inductive type. In consequence, a recursive occurrence of the
type being defined may not appear inside a quotient in an inductive definition, as it may
inside a <code>List</code>:<ref name="refman-quot" />

<pre class="lean lean-fails" style="background: #f8f9fa; border: 1px solid #c8ccd1; padding: 0.6em; margin: 0.3em 0; font-size: 0.85em; line-height: 1.35; overflow-x: auto; white-space: pre;">
inductive SetTree (α : Type u) where
  | leaf : α → SetTree α
  | branch : Quot (fun (xs ys : List (SetTree α)) => True) → SetTree α
</pre>

Lean rejects it with a message marked <code>(kernel)</code>: the second argument of
<code>'SetTree.branch'</code> contains a non valid occurrence of the datatypes being declared. The reference manual's remedy is to define the
type without the nested quotient and then quotient the whole type by a relation that
identifies the intended trees.<ref name="refman-quot" />

Quotients are also one of the places where the checker's algorithm and the type theory part
company. Carneiro shows that a quotient of a proposition behaves like a subsingleton
eliminator, and with it gives an instance where the checker's definitional-equality test
is not transitive.<ref name="carneiro" /> The page on
[[Lean theorem prover/Foundations/Proof irrelevance and subsingleton elimination|proof irrelevance and subsingleton elimination]]
treats the main case of this, which comes from the accessibility predicate.

Other proof assistants make different choices. Carneiro noted in 2019 that Coq had no quotient
types with a computation rule, so that its users worked with setoids, types paired with an
equivalence relation that stands in for equality.<ref name="carneiro" />
